name: Students With Disabilities and English Learners
title: Students With Disabilities and English Learners
answer: This idea is about using AI practice tools to support students with disabilities and English learners in kindergarten through 12th grade mathematics. It matters because adaptive repetition, simplified word problems, and read aloud can remove barriers while keeping the math skill the same. Schools still need to check whether these groups benefit and keep IEP teams and teachers in charge of goals and language demand.

sections.body: AI practice tools can be especially useful for students who need more repetition or a different pace. For students with disabilities, math practice can adapt by slowing down, repeating a step, or offering a visual model when a student struggles. For English learners, a word problem can be a barrier even when the math is within reach. A teacher can use an approved tool to create versions of the same problem with simpler sentence structure, defined key terms, and a picture where it helps. The math stays the same, so the student practices the skill without being blocked by language.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In kindergarten through 12th grade math, the text does not give separate grade bands. For students with disabilities, adaptive practice can slow the pace, repeat a step, or show a visual model when a student struggles, and the individualized education program team decides how the tool fits that student's goals. For English learners, a teacher can use an approved tool to make versions of the same word problem with simpler sentences, key terms defined, and a picture where it helps. The math stays exactly the same, so the student practices the skill without being blocked by language. Over time, the teacher raises the language demand as the student's English grows, and read aloud supports such as Microsoft Immersive Reader let a student who struggles with reading focus on the math.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives one evidence label for this idea: A review of 29 studies of AI with students with disabilities found a medium sized positive effect across subjects (Zhang, 2024). That review covers students with disabilities across subjects, not mathematics alone. For the English learner adaptations and read aloud supports described here, the text gives no study, so those parts rest on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The individualized education program team decides how the tool fits each student's goals, and teachers should use approved tools. The question is always which skill the lesson is building, so reading support usually opens access rather than skipping needed practice. In any pilot, results for students with disabilities and English learners should be watched closely. An average gain across a class can hide a group that is falling behind, so teachers should look separately at how these students do on checks without the tool. If a tool helps most students but not these groups, it needs adjustment before it spreads.
